components.description: Spreads requests across the replicas of its targets (round-robin, least-connections or random). Links can filter by request type, e.g. to route reads and writes differently.

ports.name: out
ports.label: Targets
ports.description: Instances to balance across. A retry (link max attempts > 1) avoids the instance that just failed.

fields.label: Technology
fields.description: Product or managed service. It sets the upstream timeout and circuit breakers shown under Technology behaviour; presets also fill in typical numbers.

fields.label: Balancing policy
fields.description: How a target instance is chosen. Instances are the replicas of every linked target that carries the request type.

fields.label: Overhead
fields.description: Processing overhead added per request by the balancer itself (ms).

fields.label: Max connections
fields.description: Concurrent requests the balancer accepts; beyond this new requests are rejected.

fields.label: Rate limit
fields.description: Requests per second admitted (token bucket); excess requests are rejected (HTTP 429). Empty = no limit.

fields.label: Burst
fields.description: Bucket size: requests admitted in a burst above the rate. Empty = one second's worth.

fields.label: Upstream timeout
fields.description: How long the balancer waits for a target's response before answering 504 itself, unless the link has a shorter timeout. Empty = the technology's default (nginx 60 s, Envoy 15 s, API Gateway 29 s, ALB 60 s; none for HAProxy and generic).

fields.label: Circuit breaker: max requests per target
fields.description: Requests in flight to one target (upstream cluster) before new ones get 503 immediately (Envoy circuit breakers, 1,024 by default). Empty = technology default.

fields.label: CPU
fields.description: vCPU per instance. Empty = not modelled. Shown on the design and used for price estimates; it does not change the simulation.

fields.label: Memory
fields.description: Memory per instance (GiB). Empty = not modelled. Shown on the design and used for price estimates; it does not change the simulation.

fields.label: Cost per hour
fields.description: Price of the balancer per hour, in USD. Illustrative default; use your provider's pricing.

modeled: Instance selection per policy across all routable replicas of linked targets (follows autoscaling)
Per-link timeout and retries that avoid the failed instance
Technology defaults: upstream timeout (504) and Envoy circuit breakers (503)
Connection limit (rejects beyond max connections)
Optional rate limit (token bucket); excess rejected as rate_limited
notModeled: Health checks and ejection
TLS handshakes
Sticky sessions
Per-client or per-route rate limits

presets.name: Nginx
presets.description: Reverse proxy with very low per-request overhead: 2 workers x 1,024 connections, two per proxied request, so 1,024 requests at once; 60 s upstream timeout.

presets.name: HAProxy
presets.description: High-performance TCP/HTTP load balancer, least-connections balancing.

presets.name: Envoy
presets.description: Service proxy (also the data plane of most service meshes): circuit breakers at 1,024 requests per target, 15 s route timeout.

presets.name: Kong API gateway
presets.description: API gateway in front of services, with a global rate limit.

presets.name: ALB-style load balancer
presets.description: Managed cloud application load balancer (illustrative numbers, not a vendor benchmark).

presets.name: API-gateway-style (managed)
presets.description: Managed API gateway: higher overhead per request and an account-level rate limit.

nginx.title: Upstream read timeout 60 s
nginx.detail: nginx gives up on an upstream response after proxy_read_timeout (60 s by default) and returns 504.

nginx.title: Two connections per proxied request
nginx.detail: worker_connections counts every connection, including those to upstream servers, so each proxied request uses two and a worker serves half as many requests (the preset sizes it that way).

envoy.title: Circuit breakers (1,024 requests)
envoy.detail: Each upstream cluster allows 1,024 concurrent requests by default; beyond that Envoy answers 503 at once instead of queueing.

envoy.title: Route timeout 15 s
envoy.detail: A route waits 15 s for the upstream response by default, then returns 504.

aws_alb.title: Idle timeout 60 s
aws_alb.detail: The load balancer closes a connection idle for 60 s (default), which ends a slow upstream response with 504.

api_gateway.title: Integration timeout 29 s
api_gateway.detail: The gateway waits at most 29 s for the backend by default, then returns 504 (regional and private REST APIs can request more).

api_gateway.title: Account throttle
api_gateway.detail: 10,000 requests per second with a 5,000 burst per account and Region by default (token bucket; lower in some newer Regions); excess gets 429. The preset sets these.

kong.title: Upstream timeouts 60 s
kong.detail: A Kong service waits 60 s (read_timeout) for the upstream by default.

components.description: Stateless application servers. Each replica has a worker pool and a bounded queue. Outgoing links are called in order for matching request types (e.g. reads to the cache, writes to the database). Runs on VMs, containers, Kubernetes (optional autoscaling) or as a serverless function.

ports.name: out
ports.label: Dependencies
ports.description: Downstream calls made while handling a request. Each link's request types decide which requests use it.

fields.label: Technology
fields.description: Runtime or framework. It sets the concurrency model (event loop for Node.js), GC pauses, JIT warm-up and serverless cold starts, shown under Technology behaviour.

fields.label: Platform
fields.description: Where it runs. VM and Docker behave the same (fixed replicas unless autoscaling is on); Kubernetes usually pairs with autoscaling (HPA); serverless runs one request per instance with cold starts and a concurrency limit.

fields.label: Replicas
fields.description: Number of identical instances. Each has its own workers and queue. With autoscaling: the starting count.

fields.label: Workers per replica
fields.description: Requests one replica processes concurrently (threads/worker processes). Event-loop runtimes (Node.js) use the processes per replica instead.

fields.label: Queue limit per replica
fields.description: Requests that may wait for a free worker per replica; more are rejected (HTTP 503).

fields.label: Queue timeout
fields.description: Requests waiting longer than this for a worker are rejected (ms). Empty = no limit.

fields.label: Service time
fields.description: Handler time per request on a worker, excluding downstream calls (ms). This is an assumption unless calibrated from telemetry.

fields.label: Workers block on downstream calls
fields.description: On: a worker stays occupied while waiting for downstream calls (thread-per-request). Off: the worker is released during downstream I/O (async/event-loop servers).

fields.label: CPU
fields.description: vCPU per replica. Empty = not modelled. When set, CPU work waits for a free core while more handlers than cores want the CPU (CPU contention); below 1 (e.g. 0.5) CPU work runs proportionally slower. Service time is treated as CPU work. Serverless: one request per instance, so only values below 1 matter.

fields.label: Memory
fields.description: Memory per replica (GiB). Empty = not modelled. When set, every request a replica holds (queued, running or waiting on downstream calls) uses memory; a request that would exceed it is refused (out of memory).

fields.label: Memory per request
fields.description: Memory one in-flight request uses (MiB). Only used when memory is set.

fields.label: Memory at idle
fields.description: Memory a replica uses before any request (runtime, heap, caches) (MiB). Only used when memory is set.

fields.label: Autoscaling
fields.description: Add and remove replicas to keep utilization near the target (like a Kubernetes Horizontal Pod Autoscaler). Ignored on the serverless platform.

fields.label: Min replicas
fields.description: Fewest replicas autoscaling keeps running.

fields.label: Max replicas
fields.description: Most replicas autoscaling may run.

fields.label: Target utilization
fields.description: Utilization the autoscaler aims for: the share of busy workers, or of the CPU size when the replica has one (whichever is higher), like the Kubernetes HPA's CPU target.

fields.label: Evaluation interval
fields.description: How often the autoscaler re-evaluates (s). Scale-down waits for 3 consecutive low readings.

fields.label: Replica start-up time
fields.description: Time from the scale-up decision until a new replica takes traffic (pod scheduling, image pull, start-up, readiness).

fields.label: Concurrency limit
fields.description: Most instances (= concurrent requests) the function may run; beyond it requests are throttled.

fields.label: Cold start
fields.description: Extra time for a request that has to start a new instance (ms). Empty = the runtime's typical cold start (Java about 1.2 s, Node.js and Python about 250 ms, Go about 100 ms; illustrative).

fields.label: Cluster
fields.description: The Kubernetes cluster (a cluster part in this design) whose nodes run this service's pods. Empty = the only cluster in the design, if there is exactly one.

fields.label: Scale-out rate per 10 s
fields.description: New instances the platform may start per 10 seconds (AWS Lambda: 1,000); requests that would need more are throttled.

fields.label: Concurrency model
fields.description: thread_pool: each worker handles one request at a time. event_loop: each process runs every request's CPU work on one thread, one piece at a time, and waits for I/O without blocking (Node.js). Auto follows the technology.

fields.label: Event-loop processes per replica
fields.description: Event-loop processes per replica (Node.js cluster mode, PM2, uvicorn workers).

fields.label: GC pause
fields.description: Median stop-the-world pause per garbage collection (ms); every request on the replica stalls meanwhile. Empty = runtime default (Java about 12, .NET 6, Node.js 2, Go 0.1, Rust 0; illustrative).

fields.label: Requests between GCs
fields.description: Requests a replica serves between collections (allocation pressure). Empty = runtime default.

fields.label: JIT warm-up slowdown
fields.description: How much slower a freshly started instance runs before the JIT has optimised it (applies to replicas started during the run and to serverless instances). Empty = runtime default (Java 2.5x, .NET 1.5x, others 1x; illustrative).

fields.label: JIT warm-up time
fields.description: Time for a new instance to reach full speed (s), fading linearly. Empty = runtime default.

fields.label: Keep warm
fields.description: Idle time after which an instance is reclaimed (s); the next request needs a cold start.

fields.label: Cost per replica-hour
fields.description: Price of one replica (or serverless instance) per hour, in USD. Illustrative default; use your provider's pricing.

modeled: FIFO queue per replica with a size limit and a wait timeout
Worker pool per replica; service time sampled from the configured distribution
Technology behaviour: event loops (Node.js), stop-the-world GC pauses, JIT warm-up of new instances, runtime-specific serverless cold starts
Sequential downstream calls; blocking (thread-per-request) or non-blocking I/O
Autoscaling (when on): utilization-driven replica count with evaluation interval, start-up delay and scale-down stabilization
Serverless (platform): one request per instance, cold starts, concurrency limit and scale-out rate (throttling), idle reclaim
CPU cores (when set): service time needs a core; with fewer cores than workers, work queues for a core
Memory (when set): requests held by a replica use memory; past the limit new requests are refused
notModeled: OOM kills and restarts (memory is a refusal limit instead); concurrent GC CPU overhead
Parallel fan-out calls (dependencies are called one after another)
Node/cluster capacity limits for new pods, readiness probe failures
Serverless memory-to-CPU scaling (set CPU directly) and provisioned concurrency

presets.name: Generic service (VM)
presets.description: Fixed replicas on virtual machines, thread-per-request workers.

presets.name: Java/Spring on Docker
presets.description: Spring Boot containers with a large blocking thread pool (Tomcat-style).

presets.name: Node.js on Docker
presets.description: One event loop per container: every request's CPU work queues for that single thread, while I/O waits don't hold it.

presets.name: Go service on Kubernetes (HPA)
presets.description: Go pods behind a Kubernetes Service with a Horizontal Pod Autoscaler.

presets.name: Python service on Kubernetes (HPA)
presets.description: Gunicorn-style worker processes in pods, autoscaled by an HPA.

presets.name: Serverless function (Lambda-style)
presets.description: Function-as-a-service: an instance per concurrent request, cold starts when scaling out.

nodejs.title: Single-threaded event loop
nodejs.detail: JavaScript runs on one thread per process: CPU work of every request queues for that one loop (event-loop lag), while I/O waits don't hold it. Add processes per replica (cluster mode) to use more cores.

nodejs.title: Short GC pauses
nodejs.detail: V8's scavenger pauses the loop for a couple of milliseconds now and then (illustrative).

java.title: Thread per request
java.detail: Spring MVC on Tomcat serves each request on a pool thread (200 by default) that stays busy during downstream calls.

java.title: Stop-the-world GC pauses
java.detail: The garbage collector (G1 by default) pauses all application threads for a few milliseconds when the young generation fills up, more often under load (pause and frequency are illustrative).

java.title: JIT warm-up
java.detail: A new instance starts with interpreted or lightly optimised code and runs slower until the JIT has compiled the hot paths (factor and duration are illustrative).

dotnet.title: Tiered compilation warm-up
dotnet.detail: Methods start unoptimised and are recompiled once hot, so a fresh instance is slower at first (factor and duration are illustrative).

dotnet.title: GC pauses
dotnet.detail: Gen0 collections pause managed threads briefly (illustrative).

go.title: Goroutines on every core
go.detail: Requests run as goroutines scheduled across all cores; the concurrent GC's stop-the-world pauses are usually under 100 microseconds.

rust.title: No garbage collector
rust.detail: Memory is freed deterministically: no GC pauses and no JIT warm-up.

python.title: Worker processes
python.detail: Gunicorn-style sync workers handle one request each; each process is held to one core by the GIL (the docs suggest 2 x cores + 1 workers).

php.title: Process per request (PHP-FPM)
php.detail: Each request takes a PHP-FPM child; pm.max_children (5 in the shipped www.conf) caps concurrency and memory is freed when the request ends.

components.description: Cache-aside: reads that hit return from memory; misses continue through the 'miss' port to the data store, then optionally repopulate the cache. Writes invalidate the key.

ports.name: miss
ports.label: Miss
ports.description: Where reads go when the key is not cached (usually the database).

fields.label: Technology
fields.description: The cache product. It sets how commands execute (one thread for Redis and Valkey, worker threads for Memcached) and the eviction behaviour, shown under Technology behaviour. Presets also fill in typical numbers.

fields.label: Hit model
fields.description: fixed_ratio: each read hits with the given probability (simplest assumption). ttl_keyspace: reads pick keys from the workload's Zipf keyspace; a key hits if it was filled less than TTL seconds ago (derives hit rate, including cold start).

fields.label: Hit ratio
fields.description: Probability a read is served from the cache (fixed_ratio model).

fields.label: TTL
fields.description: Time a filled key stays valid (ttl_keyspace model). Capacity is unbounded (no eviction).

fields.label: Populate on miss
fields.description: After a miss is served by the data store, write the value back (one extra cache operation).

fields.label: Command time
fields.description: Time to execute one cache command, excluding network (ms).

fields.label: Command executors
fields.description: Commands executed in parallel per shard (Memcached threads, CDN or Varnish parallelism). Ignored when commands run single-threaded (Redis, Valkey).

fields.label: Shards (cluster nodes)
fields.description: Cache nodes the keys are split across (Redis Cluster shards, Memcached servers). Each has its own executors and memory; keys hash to a shard, so a hot key loads one.

fields.label: Single-threaded commands
fields.description: Execute commands one at a time per shard, whatever the cores. Auto: on for Redis and Valkey.

fields.label: Eviction policy
fields.description: When memory is full (TTL model with memory set): allkeys_lru evicts the least recently used key; noeviction (Redis's own default) refuses new keys with an out-of-memory error, so missed reads cannot be cached. Auto: allkeys_lru.

fields.label: Persistence
fields.description: rdb: snapshot to disk every interval; forking the process blocks commands for about the fork time per GiB of data. Auto: none (cache use).

fields.label: Snapshot interval
fields.description: Time between RDB snapshots (s).

fields.label: Fork stall per GiB
fields.description: Command stall per GiB of data while forking for a snapshot (ms). Typical Linux hosts: around 10; some virtual machines much more.

fields.label: Queue limit
fields.description: Commands that may wait for an executor; more are rejected.

fields.label: Queue timeout
fields.description: Commands waiting longer than this are rejected (ms). Empty = no limit.

fields.label: CPU
fields.description: vCPU per cache node. Empty = not modelled. When set, CPU work waits for a free core while more handlers than cores want the CPU (CPU contention); below 1 (e.g. 0.5) CPU work runs proportionally slower.

fields.label: Memory
fields.description: Memory per cache node (GiB). Empty = not modelled. 80% of it holds keys. TTL model: when it is full the least recently used key is evicted. Fixed hit ratio: checked against the workload's keyspace.

fields.label: Item size
fields.description: Average size of one cached key and value, with overhead (KiB). Only used when memory is set.

fields.label: Cost per hour
fields.description: Price of the cache per hour, used for cost estimates only. Illustrative default.

modeled: Hit/miss decision per read (fixed probability or TTL over a Zipf keyspace)
Technology behaviour: single-threaded commands (Redis, Valkey) or worker threads (Memcached)
Cluster shards: keys hash to a shard with its own executors and memory
Miss path latency added to the caller; repopulation cost
Memory (when set, TTL model): key capacity per shard, LRU eviction or noeviction out-of-memory errors
RDB snapshots (when on): fork stalls block commands for a time proportional to the data
CPU cores (when set): commands queue for a core when executors outnumber cores
notModeled: LFU and other eviction policies; memory for the fixed-ratio model (checked, not simulated)
Thundering herd / request coalescing on misses
Replicas and failover; copy-on-write memory growth during snapshots
CDN geography (edge-to-user latency belongs on the incoming link)

presets.name: Redis
presets.description: Single Redis node: commands run on one thread, sub-millisecond; extra cores do not add command throughput. Illustrative defaults.

presets.name: Valkey
presets.description: Redis-compatible; I/O threads take socket work off the command thread, so each command is shorter, but commands still run one at a time. Illustrative defaults.

presets.name: Memcached
presets.description: Multi-threaded get/set cache with its default 4 worker threads. Illustrative defaults.

presets.name: CDN edge cache
presets.description: Edge cache in front of the origin: huge parallelism, a few ms per request, most reads served at the edge. Put user-to-edge latency on the incoming link. Illustrative defaults.

presets.name: Varnish
presets.description: Reverse-proxy HTTP cache in front of the application. Illustrative defaults.

redis.title: One thread executes commands
redis.detail: Commands run one at a time on a single thread per node, however many cores it has; scale out with cluster shards (keys are split across 16,384 hash slots).

redis.title: Eviction policy
redis.detail: With allkeys-lru the least recently used keys make room for new ones; with noeviction (Redis's own default) writes fail with an out-of-memory error once memory is full.

redis.title: Snapshot fork stalls
redis.detail: With RDB snapshots on, each snapshot forks the process; the fork blocks the command thread for about 10-13 ms per GB of data on modern hardware (Redis's own measurements), far more on some older virtual machines.

valkey.title: One thread executes commands
valkey.detail: Valkey offloads socket I/O to I/O threads, which shortens each command, but commands still execute one at a time per node; scale out with cluster shards.

valkey.title: Eviction policy
valkey.detail: With allkeys-lru the least recently used keys make room for new ones; with noeviction (Redis's own default) writes fail with an out-of-memory error once memory is full.

valkey.title: Snapshot fork stalls
valkey.detail: With RDB snapshots on, each snapshot forks the process; the fork blocks the command thread for about 10-13 ms per GB of data on modern hardware (Redis's own measurements), far more on some older virtual machines.

memcached.title: Multi-threaded
memcached.detail: Worker threads (4 by default) execute requests in parallel; memory is managed in slabs with LRU eviction and nothing is persisted.

components.description: Executes read and write queries on a limited number of connections per instance, and behaves like the technology you pick: row locks and group commit for relational databases, majority writes for MongoDB, capacity units for DynamoDB, fan-out searches for Elasticsearch, replicas that lag.

fields.label: Technology
fields.description: The database product. It sets how the database behaves (locks, commit, replication, read routing, partition limits...), shown under Technology behaviour, where every setting can be overridden. Presets also fill in typical numbers.

fields.label: Max connections per instance
fields.description: Queries executing concurrently on one instance (connection pool size / backend workers). Every primary and replica in every shard has its own limit.

fields.label: Read query time
fields.description: Execution time of a read query on one instance (ms).

fields.label: Write query time
fields.description: Execution time of a write on one instance, before the log flush and replica acknowledgements (ms).

fields.label: Read replicas
fields.description: Copies per shard that replay the primary's writes (replicas, secondaries). Writes always go to the primary; which instances serve reads depends on 'Reads served by'.

fields.label: Shards (partitions)
fields.description: Partitions of the data, each with its own primary (and replicas). Requests are routed by hashing the key, so popular keys concentrate load on one shard. DynamoDB-style capacity units derive the partition count instead.

fields.label: Replication factor
fields.description: Copies of each item kept by a leaderless or consensus store (e.g. Cassandra, distributed SQL). Combined with the consistency level it decides how many replica responses an operation waits for.

fields.label: Consistency level
fields.description: Replica responses an operation waits for when the replication factor is above 1: one, a majority (quorum) or all. Latency becomes the k-th fastest of the replicas.

fields.label: Throughput limit per shard
fields.description: Provisioned throughput per shard (operations/s, bursts up to one second's worth). Requests above it are throttled. Empty = no limit.

fields.label: Wait queue limit
fields.description: Queries that may wait for a connection on one instance; more are rejected.

fields.label: Acquire timeout
fields.description: Connection acquire timeout (ms). Queries waiting longer are rejected. Empty = no limit.

fields.label: Row locks on writes
fields.description: Writes to the same key (row or document) take a lock: a second write waits until the first commits, holding its connection meanwhile. Auto: on for relational databases and MongoDB, off for Cassandra, DynamoDB and search engines.

fields.label: Reads wait for writers
fields.description: A read of a key that is being written waits for the writer's lock (SQL Server's default READ COMMITTED). Auto: on for SQL Server; MVCC databases read the last committed version instead.

fields.label: Commits wait for the log flush
fields.description: Each write waits for the write-ahead log (or journal) to reach disk. Commits that arrive during a flush share the next one (group commit). Auto: on for relational databases and MongoDB.

fields.label: Log flush time
fields.description: Time of one log flush (fsync) on the storage (ms). Network block storage is slower than local NVMe.

fields.label: Replica writes
fields.description: How writes reach the replicas. async: the primary commits, replicas replay later (replication lag, stale reads). majority: the write also waits until a majority of the copies have it (MongoDB's default write concern). all: it waits for every replica (Elasticsearch). none: replicas only serve reads.

fields.label: Replica apply workers
fields.description: Workers a replica uses to replay writes. Empty = the technology's default (PostgreSQL 1, MySQL 4, MongoDB 16).

fields.label: Replay cost vs. write time
fields.description: Replaying a write on a replica costs this share of the write's execution time.

fields.label: Replication network delay
fields.description: Network delay shipping a write (and an acknowledgement) between primary and replicas (ms).

fields.label: Reads served by
fields.description: Which instances serve reads: all (round-robin over primary and replicas), the primary only (MongoDB's default read preference) or the replicas only (secondaryPreferred). Auto follows the technology.

fields.label: Concurrent reads (tickets)
fields.description: Read operations one instance runs at once, beyond the connection limit (MongoDB WiredTiger: 128). Empty = the technology's default (none for most).

fields.label: Concurrent writes (tickets)
fields.description: Write operations one instance runs at once (MongoDB WiredTiger: 128). Empty = technology default.

fields.label: Reads sent to every shard
fields.description: Share of reads that do not target one shard and go to every shard, waiting for the slowest (searches; MongoDB queries without the shard key). Empty = technology default (Elasticsearch: every search).

fields.label: Router / coordinator time
fields.description: Routing or merging time added per operation when sharded or scattering (mongos, Elasticsearch coordinating node) (ms). Empty = technology default.

fields.label: SSTables per cold read
fields.description: Log-structured stores (Cassandra, Scylla): disk reads a buffer-cache miss costs, because a row can be spread over several SSTables. Empty = technology default.

fields.label: Capacity units and partition limits
fields.description: Meter reads and writes in capacity units with per-partition limits (3,000 read and 1,000 write units per second each), DynamoDB-style. Auto: on for DynamoDB.

fields.label: Capacity mode
fields.description: On-demand: the table serves up to 12,000 read and 4,000 write units per second from the start. Provisioned: the units below, plus up to 300 s of banked burst.

fields.label: Read capacity units
fields.description: Provisioned read capacity units per second for the table.

fields.label: Write capacity units
fields.description: Provisioned write capacity units per second for the table.

fields.label: Item size
fields.description: Average item size (KB): a read costs one unit per 4 KB, a write one per 1 KB.

fields.label: Read consistency
fields.description: Eventually consistent reads cost half a unit (the default); strongly consistent reads a full unit.

fields.label: CPU
fields.description: vCPU per instance. Empty = not modelled. When set, CPU work waits for a free core while more handlers than cores want the CPU (CPU contention); below 1 (e.g. 0.5) CPU work runs proportionally slower. Only the CPU share of each query needs a core.

fields.label: CPU share of query time
fields.description: Share of query time that needs a CPU core; the rest is I/O, locks and network. Only used when CPU is set.

fields.label: Memory
fields.description: Memory per instance (GiB). Empty = not modelled. With a working set, 75% of it is buffer cache: reads of data that does not fit go to disk.

fields.label: Hot working set
fields.description: Size of the data that is read often (GiB), across all shards. With memory set, the share of reads served from memory is min(1, 75% of memory / working set per shard).

fields.label: Disk read time
fields.description: Extra time of a read that misses the buffer cache and goes to disk (ms).

fields.label: Storage
fields.description: Disk per instance (GiB). Empty = not modelled. Checked against the data size: each instance stores its shard's data.

fields.label: Data size
fields.description: Total data stored (GiB), across all shards. Used to check storage (and DynamoDB partitions).

fields.label: Cost per instance-hour
fields.description: Price of one instance (primary or replica, per shard) per hour, used for cost estimates only. Illustrative default; use your own price.

modeled: Connection limit with a bounded wait queue and acquire timeout, per instance
Technology behaviour: row/document locks, group commit, replica replay with lag and stale reads, majority or all-replica write acknowledgements, read routing, concurrency tickets
Key-hash sharding; a skewed (Zipf) keyspace creates hot shards and hot rows
Scatter-gather reads across every shard (searches, queries without the shard key)
Capacity units with per-partition limits and burst capacity (DynamoDB-style)
Replication factor + consistency level: latency is the k-th fastest of RF replicas
CPU cores (when set): the CPU share of each query (and of replica replay) needs a core
Buffer cache (memory and working set set): cold reads pay disk reads (several SSTables for LSM stores)
Storage (with a data size): checked per instance
notModeled: Deadlocks, lock escalation and range (gap) locks; vacuum, checkpoints and compaction
Failover and leader election
Query planning, cross-shard transactions and rebalancing
Adaptive capacity moving throughput between DynamoDB partitions

presets.name: PostgreSQL
presets.description: Single PostgreSQL primary behind an application connection pool: row locks, group commit on the write-ahead log. Numbers are illustrative assumptions, not vendor benchmarks.

presets.name: PostgreSQL + 2 read replicas
presets.description: Primary for writes, two streaming replicas that share the reads and replay the write-ahead log on one worker each (lag under heavy writes). Numbers are illustrative assumptions, not vendor benchmarks.

presets.name: MySQL
presets.description: Single MySQL (InnoDB) primary: row locks, binary log group commit. Numbers are illustrative assumptions, not vendor benchmarks.

presets.name: SQL Server
presets.description: Single SQL Server instance with the default READ COMMITTED locking: reads of a row being written wait. The hourly price includes a licence. Numbers are illustrative assumptions, not vendor benchmarks.

presets.name: CockroachDB-style distributed SQL
presets.description: Three ranges/shards, each replicated three times with quorum (Raft) writes: survives a node loss, pays a consensus round trip. Numbers are illustrative assumptions, not vendor benchmarks.

presets.name: MongoDB replica set
presets.description: Primary plus two secondaries. Writes wait for a majority (the default write concern); reads use the secondaries (secondaryPreferred). Numbers are illustrative assumptions, not vendor benchmarks.

presets.name: MongoDB sharded cluster
presets.description: Four shards, each a replica set, behind mongos. Operations with the shard key go to one shard; 10% of reads lack it and are broadcast to all four. Numbers are illustrative assumptions, not vendor benchmarks.

presets.name: Cassandra
presets.description: Six token ranges, replication factor 3, QUORUM reads and writes. LSM storage makes writes cheaper than reads. Numbers are illustrative assumptions, not vendor benchmarks.

presets.name: DynamoDB-style key-value store
presets.description: Managed key-value table in on-demand mode: capacity units with per-partition limits, so a hot key is throttled. The hourly price stands in for the request charges. Numbers are illustrative assumptions, not vendor benchmarks.

presets.name: Elasticsearch
presets.description: Three primary shards with one replica each. Every search hits all three shards; the search thread pool (7 threads for 4 cores) and its 1,000-request queue (Elasticsearch 8 defaults) reject the excess with 429. Numbers are illustrative assumptions, not vendor benchmarks.

postgresql.title: Row locks on writes
postgresql.detail: Two writes to the same row (key) cannot run at once: the second waits until the first commits, holding its connection while it waits. With a skewed keyspace the hottest rows become a queue of their own.

postgresql.title: Readers never wait for writers
postgresql.detail: Multi-version concurrency control: a read sees the last committed version instead of waiting for a row lock.

postgresql.title: Commits wait for the log flush (group commit)
postgresql.detail: A write is durable only when the write-ahead log reaches disk. Commits that arrive while a flush is running share the next flush, so write throughput is not capped by fsyncs, but every write waits up to about 1.5 flushes.

postgresql.title: Asynchronous replicas with lag
postgresql.detail: Replicas replay the primary's log after the commit, on a limited number of workers (in PostgreSQL a single startup process replays the WAL), so under heavy writes the lag grows and replica reads can return stale data.

sqlserver.title: Readers wait for writers
sqlserver.detail: Under the default READ COMMITTED isolation (without read committed snapshot) a read of a row that is being written waits for the writer's exclusive lock.

cockroachdb.title: Row locks on writes
cockroachdb.detail: Two writes to the same row (key) cannot run at once: the second waits until the first commits, holding its connection while it waits. With a skewed keyspace the hottest rows become a queue of their own.

cockroachdb.title: Consensus writes (Raft)
cockroachdb.detail: Every write is replicated to a majority of the range's replicas (3 by default) before it commits: set the replication factor and quorum consistency to see the cost.

cockroachdb.title: Commits wait for the log flush (group commit)
cockroachdb.detail: A write is durable only when the write-ahead log reaches disk. Commits that arrive while a flush is running share the next flush, so write throughput is not capped by fsyncs, but every write waits up to about 1.5 flushes.

yugabytedb.title: Row locks on writes
yugabytedb.detail: Two writes to the same row (key) cannot run at once: the second waits until the first commits, holding its connection while it waits. With a skewed keyspace the hottest rows become a queue of their own.

yugabytedb.title: Commits wait for the log flush (group commit)

mongodb.title: Document-level concurrency
mongodb.detail: WiredTiger lets writes to different documents run in parallel; two writes to the same document conflict and one waits.

mongodb.title: Concurrent transaction tickets
mongodb.detail: Each node runs at most 128 read and 128 write storage-engine transactions at once (since 7.0 MongoDB adjusts the limit dynamically, never above 128); more queue inside the server even when connections are free.

mongodb.title: Write concern "majority" by default
mongodb.detail: A write is acknowledged only after a majority of the replica set has it (the implicit default for replica sets without arbiters), so every write waits for the fastest secondary; slow or lagging secondaries slow writes down.

mongodb.title: Reads go to the primary by default
mongodb.detail: The default read preference is primary: secondaries only serve reads when you choose secondaryPreferred (read from replicas).

mongodb.title: Router hop and broadcast queries when sharded
mongodb.detail: With shards, mongos routes each operation; queries without the shard key are sent to every shard and wait for the slowest.

cassandra.title: Cheap writes (log-structured storage)
cassandra.detail: Writes append to the commit log and an in-memory table: no read before write, no row locks, and the commit log syncs periodically rather than per write.

cassandra.title: Reads merge several SSTables
cassandra.detail: A read that misses memory may touch more than one SSTable on disk (2 on average here, illustrative), so cold reads cost more than writes.

dynamodb.title: Per-partition throughput limits
dynamodb.detail: Each partition serves at most 3,000 read units and 1,000 write units per second. Keys hash to partitions, so a hot key is throttled even when the table has capacity left.

dynamodb.title: Capacity units
dynamodb.detail: A strongly consistent read of up to 4 KB costs 1 read unit (eventually consistent: half); a write of up to 1 KB costs 1 write unit. Requests beyond the table's capacity are throttled.

dynamodb.title: Burst capacity
dynamodb.detail: Provisioned tables bank up to 300 seconds of unused capacity and spend it on spikes (here the bank starts full).

elasticsearch.title: Every search hits every shard
elasticsearch.detail: A search runs on one copy of each shard and the coordinating node merges the results, so search latency follows the slowest shard and each search costs one query per shard.

elasticsearch.title: Index writes wait for replicas
elasticsearch.detail: An indexing operation is acknowledged after the primary and its in-sync replicas have it.

elasticsearch.title: Bounded thread pools (HTTP 429)
elasticsearch.detail: Searches run on a fixed pool of (cores x 3 / 2) + 1 threads with a bounded queue (1,000 in 8.x, 1,000 per thread since 9.0); past it the node rejects with 429. The preset sizes connections and queue that way.

opensearch.title: Every search hits every shard
opensearch.detail: A search runs on one copy of each shard and the coordinating node merges the results, so search latency follows the slowest shard and each search costs one query per shard.

opensearch.title: Index writes wait for replicas
opensearch.detail: An indexing operation is acknowledged after the primary and its in-sync replicas have it.

opensearch.title: Bounded thread pools (HTTP 429)
opensearch.detail: Searches run on a fixed pool of (cores x 3 / 2) + 1 threads with a bounded queue (1,000 in 8.x, 1,000 per thread since 9.0); past it the node rejects with 429. The preset sizes connections and queue that way.

components.description: A third-party service you call but do not operate (payments, email, SMS, identity, LLM inference, object storage). Each call takes the provider's response time, may fail, and may be rejected by the provider's rate or concurrency limit.

fields.label: Kind of service
fields.description: Kind of provider. A label only; presets set latency, error rate, limits and price to illustrative defaults.

fields.label: Response time
fields.description: Time the provider takes to answer one call, excluding network to it (ms).

fields.label: Error rate
fields.description: Share of calls the provider fails (5xx / errors), after its response time.

fields.label: Rate limit
fields.description: Calls per second the provider accepts (bursts up to one second's worth); more are rejected as rate limited. Empty = no limit.

fields.label: Concurrency limit
fields.description: Calls that may be in flight at once; more are rejected as throttled. Empty = no limit.

fields.label: Cost per million calls
fields.description: Price per million calls, used for cost estimates only. Illustrative default.

modeled: Response time sampled from the configured distribution
Random provider errors at the configured rate
Provider rate limit (token bucket) and concurrency limit; excess calls fail immediately
Price per million calls for cost estimates
notModeled: Provider-side queueing and degradation under your load
Retry-After headers and provider-side backoff
Regional outages (use a fault to inject one)

presets.name: Payments API
presets.description: Card payment provider: a few hundred ms per charge, rare errors, per-account rate limit. Usually priced per transaction amount, so no per-call price is set. Numbers are illustrative assumptions, not a provider's published figures.

presets.name: Email API
presets.description: Transactional email sending. Numbers are illustrative assumptions, not a provider's published figures.

presets.name: SMS API
presets.description: SMS / messaging provider: slower and pricier per call. Numbers are illustrative assumptions, not a provider's published figures.

presets.name: Identity provider
presets.description: OAuth/OIDC identity provider for token checks and logins. Usually priced per active user, so no per-call price is set. Numbers are illustrative assumptions, not a provider's published figures.

presets.name: LLM inference API
presets.description: Hosted model inference: seconds per call with a heavy tail, tight rate and concurrency limits, noticeable error rate. Numbers are illustrative assumptions, not a provider's published figures.

presets.name: Object storage (S3-compatible)
presets.description: Object GETs from S3-compatible storage: tens of ms, very high limits. Numbers are illustrative assumptions, not a provider's published figures.

components.description: Asynchronous messaging (Kafka, RabbitMQ, SQS-style). Producers get an acknowledgement after publishing; consumers process messages in the background and call the outgoing links. Absorbs spikes as backlog (lag) instead of rejecting requests, and behaves like the technology you pick.

ports.name: in
ports.label: Publish
ports.description: Messages published by producers (the caller gets an ack, not the result).

ports.name: out
ports.label: Consumers
ports.description: Downstream calls each consumer makes per message, in order, for matching request types.

fields.label: Technology
fields.description: The broker or managed service. It sets how messages are partitioned, acknowledged and redelivered, shown under Technology behaviour. Presets also fill in typical numbers.

fields.label: Partitions
fields.description: Partitions (Kafka) or shards: at most one consumer works per partition, so effective consumers = min(consumers, partitions). Set it high for brokers without partitions.

fields.label: Consumers
fields.description: Concurrent consumers processing messages (consumer instances x threads).

fields.label: Max backlog
fields.description: Messages the queue holds; publishes beyond it are rejected (queue_full), or dropped silently with at-most-once delivery. Empty = unbounded.

fields.label: Publish (ack) time
fields.description: Time for the broker to accept a publish (ms), before any replication wait or batching.

fields.label: Consumer time
fields.description: Consumer handling time per message before its downstream calls (ms).

fields.label: Max deliveries
fields.description: Delivery attempts per message; after the last failure it goes to the dead-letter queue.

fields.label: Partitioning
fields.description: key: messages with the same key go to the same partition and are consumed in order by its one consumer (Kafka). round_robin: spread evenly, still one consumer per partition. none: one shared queue with competing consumers (RabbitMQ, SQS).

fields.label: Publish acknowledgement
fields.description: all: the publish waits until the replicas have the message (Kafka acks=all, the default since 3.0).

fields.label: Replication wait
fields.description: Extra publish time waiting for replicas when acks = all (ms).

fields.label: Batching linger
fields.description: The producer holds each message up to this long to batch it (Kafka linger.ms); a publish waits a uniform share of it. Empty = technology default.

fields.label: Delivery guarantee
fields.description: at_least_once: a full backlog rejects publishes. at_most_once (core NATS): the overflow is dropped silently and the publisher still gets an ack.

fields.label: Visibility timeout
fields.description: A message being processed longer than this is delivered again to another consumer (SQS visibility timeout, Pub/Sub ack deadline). Empty = technology default (SQS 30 s, Pub/Sub 10 s, none for brokers with consumer acks).

fields.label: FIFO queue
fields.description: FIFO queue (SQS): ordered, exactly-once, and limited to the publish rate below.

fields.label: FIFO publish limit
fields.description: Publishes per second a FIFO queue accepts (SQS: 300 without batching, 3,000 with); the excess is throttled.

fields.label: Memory alarm blocks publishers
fields.description: Block publishers while queued messages use more memory than the high watermark (RabbitMQ memory alarm). Needs memory set. Auto: on for RabbitMQ.

fields.label: Memory high watermark
fields.description: Share of the broker's memory queued messages may use before publishers are blocked.

fields.label: Message size
fields.description: Average message size in memory, with overhead (KiB). Used by the memory alarm.

fields.label: Brokers
fields.description: Broker nodes in the cluster (used for cost; throughput is set by consumers and partitions).

fields.label: CPU
fields.description: vCPU per broker. Empty = not modelled. Shown on the design and used for price estimates; it does not change the simulation.

fields.label: Memory
fields.description: Memory per broker (GiB). Empty = not modelled. Used by the memory alarm (RabbitMQ); otherwise shown on the design and priced.

fields.label: Storage
fields.description: Disk per broker (GiB). Empty = not modelled. Shown on the design and used for price estimates; it does not change the simulation.

fields.label: Cost per broker-hour
fields.description: Price of one broker per hour, in USD. Illustrative default; use your provider's pricing.

modeled: Publish acknowledgement latency (plus replication wait and batching linger) and a bounded backlog
Partitioned logs: key-hashed ordered partitions, one consumer each (hot partitions lag)
Shared queues: competing consumers, FIFO
Redelivery of failed messages up to max deliveries, then dead-lettering
Visibility timeouts / ack deadlines: slow processing is delivered again (duplicates)
Memory alarm flow control: publishers block past the high watermark
At-most-once delivery: overflow dropped silently; FIFO publish rate limits
Backlog (lag), consumer utilization and message age
notModeled: Broker disk and network throughput limits
Consumer group rebalancing pauses
Exactly-once transactions

presets.name: Kafka
presets.description: Partitioned log: messages hash by key to 12 ordered partitions, one consumer each; acks=all and 5 ms linger on publish.

presets.name: RabbitMQ
presets.description: Message broker with competing consumers on a queue; past the memory high watermark it blocks publishers.

presets.name: SQS-style queue
presets.description: Managed HTTP queue: slower publishes, unbounded backlog, 30 s visibility timeout (slow processing gets delivered twice).

presets.name: Pub/Sub-style topic
presets.description: Managed publish/subscribe with a 10 s ack deadline (illustrative numbers).

presets.name: NATS JetStream
presets.description: Lightweight messaging with JetStream persistence (at-least-once); switch delivery to at-most-once for core NATS.

presets.name: Redis Streams
presets.description: Append-only stream with consumer groups, in memory.

kafka.title: Ordered partitions, one consumer each
kafka.detail: Messages with the same key land on the same partition and are processed in order by the one consumer that owns it. A skewed key makes one partition, and its consumer, fall behind while others idle.

kafka.title: acks=all
kafka.detail: The producer's acknowledgement waits until the in-sync replicas have the message (the default since Kafka 3.0).

kafka.title: Batching (linger.ms)
kafka.detail: The producer holds a message up to linger.ms to batch it with others (5 ms by default in Kafka 4.0).

rabbitmq.title: Memory alarm blocks publishers
rabbitmq.detail: When queued messages use more memory than the high watermark, the broker blocks publishing connections until consumers catch up: producers slow down instead of getting errors. Needs memory and message size set.

sqs.title: Visibility timeout (30 s)
sqs.detail: A received message is hidden for the visibility timeout. If processing takes longer, the message becomes visible again and another consumer processes it too: duplicate work.

sqs.title: FIFO throughput limit
sqs.detail: FIFO queues accept about 300 publishes per second without batching; standard queues are effectively unlimited.

pubsub.title: Ack deadline (10 s)
pubsub.detail: A message not acknowledged within the ack deadline is delivered again.

nats.title: Core NATS drops, JetStream persists
nats.detail: Core NATS is at-most-once: a slow consumer's overflow is dropped and the publisher never knows. Choose at-least-once for JetStream.

components.description: A pool of nodes for services on the Kubernetes platform. Every replica becomes a pod scheduled by its CPU and memory requests; pods wait as Pending when nodes are full until the cluster autoscaler adds a node, then pull their image and start.

fields.label: Technology
fields.description: Kubernetes distribution or managed service. Presets fill in typical node sizes and provisioning times.

fields.label: Nodes
fields.description: Nodes (worker VMs) running when the simulation starts.

fields.label: vCPU per node
fields.description: vCPU per node.

fields.label: Memory per node
fields.description: Memory per node (GiB).

fields.label: Allocatable share
fields.description: Share of each node's CPU and memory left for pods after the operating system, kubelet and system daemons reserve theirs.

fields.label: Cluster autoscaler
fields.description: Add nodes for Pending pods and remove nodes left empty (Kubernetes cluster autoscaler).

fields.label: Min nodes
fields.description: Fewest nodes the cluster autoscaler keeps.

fields.label: Max nodes
fields.description: Most nodes the cluster autoscaler may run.

fields.label: Node provisioning time
fields.description: Time from the decision to add a node until it is ready for pods (VM boot, join, CNI) (s).

fields.label: Scan interval
fields.description: How often the cluster autoscaler looks for Pending pods (s). The autoscaler's default is 10 s.

fields.label: Scale-down after empty
fields.description: Time a node must stay empty before it is removed (s). The autoscaler's default is 10 minutes.

fields.label: Image pull time
fields.description: Time to pull a service's container image on a node that has not run it yet (s).

fields.label: Default CPU request
fields.description: CPU request of pods whose service sets no CPU (vCPU).

fields.label: Default memory request
fields.description: Memory request of pods whose service sets no memory (GiB).

fields.label: Cost per node-hour
fields.description: Price of one node per hour, in USD; services on the cluster are paid for through their nodes. Illustrative default.

modeled: Nodes with allocatable CPU and memory; pods bound by their requests to the least allocated node that fits
Pending pods when no node has room; scheduled as soon as room appears
Cluster autoscaler: scan interval, node provisioning delay, max/min nodes, removal of empty nodes
Image pull on the first pod of a service per node, then the service's start-up time
Services join automatically (the only cluster) or by name; each replica is a pod
notModeled: CPU contention between pods beyond their requests (noisy neighbours), limits and throttling
Pod priority and preemption, affinity, taints, topology spread
Node failures, drains and rolling deployments
Several node pools per cluster

presets.name: Kubernetes cluster
presets.description: Three 4 vCPU / 16 GiB nodes with the cluster autoscaler (up to 10 nodes, 2 minutes per node). Node sizes, provisioning times and prices are illustrative.

presets.name: EKS-style managed cluster
presets.description: Managed control plane with a node group of 4 vCPU / 16 GiB instances, about 2.5 minutes per new node. Node sizes, provisioning times and prices are illustrative.

presets.name: GKE-style managed cluster
presets.description: Managed cluster with 4 vCPU / 16 GiB nodes and node auto-provisioning, about 1.5 minutes per new node. Node sizes, provisioning times and prices are illustrative.

presets.name: AKS-style managed cluster
presets.description: Managed cluster with 4 vCPU / 16 GiB nodes, about 3 minutes per new node. Node sizes, provisioning times and prices are illustrative.

presets.name: k3s (small / edge)
presets.description: Lightweight Kubernetes on two small nodes and no cluster autoscaler: what fits is what you get. Node sizes, provisioning times and prices are illustrative.

kubernetes.title: Pods are scheduled by their requests
kubernetes.detail: Each pod reserves the CPU and memory it requests on one node; the scheduler only binds it to a node with that much unreserved, and prefers the least allocated node.

kubernetes.title: Pending pods
kubernetes.detail: When no node has room for a pod's requests it stays Pending: the replica the autoscaler asked for does not exist yet and takes no traffic.

kubernetes.title: Cluster autoscaler
kubernetes.detail: Every 10 s the cluster autoscaler looks for Pending pods and adds nodes for them; a new node takes minutes to boot and join. Nodes left empty for 10 minutes are removed.

kubernetes.title: Image pulls on new nodes
kubernetes.detail: The first pod of a service on a node pulls its container image before starting; later pods on that node reuse the cached image.

kubernetes.title: Horizontal Pod Autoscaler
kubernetes.detail: The HPA re-evaluates every 15 s by default and asks for more pods; they still have to be scheduled, pulled and started before they help.

eks.title: Pods are scheduled by their requests
eks.detail: Each pod reserves the CPU and memory it requests on one node; the scheduler only binds it to a node with that much unreserved, and prefers the least allocated node.

eks.title: Pending pods
eks.detail: When no node has room for a pod's requests it stays Pending: the replica the autoscaler asked for does not exist yet and takes no traffic.

eks.title: Cluster autoscaler
eks.detail: Every 10 s the cluster autoscaler looks for Pending pods and adds nodes for them; a new node takes minutes to boot and join. Nodes left empty for 10 minutes are removed.

eks.title: Image pulls on new nodes
eks.detail: The first pod of a service on a node pulls its container image before starting; later pods on that node reuse the cached image.

eks.title: Horizontal Pod Autoscaler

edgeFields.label: Request types
edgeFields.description: Request types carried by this link. Used for routing (e.g. reads to cache, writes to DB).

edgeFields.label: Network latency (one way)
edgeFields.description: One-way network latency in ms, applied to the request and again to the response.

edgeFields.label: Timeout
edgeFields.description: Per-attempt time the caller waits before giving up (ms). Empty = wait indefinitely.

edgeFields.label: Max attempts
edgeFields.description: Total attempts including retries (1 = no retries). Bounded to prevent retry storms from running away.

edgeFields.label: Retry backoff
edgeFields.description: Base backoff before a retry (ms); doubles on each further retry.

edgeFields.label: Call order
edgeFields.description: Call order when a service calls several dependencies for the same request (lower first).

workloadFields.label: Warm-up
workloadFields.description: Initial period excluded from summary statistics (s)

workloadFields.label: Read ratio
workloadFields.description: Fraction of requests that are reads

workloadFields.label: Arrival process
workloadFields.description: poisson: random (exponential) inter-arrivals; deterministic: evenly spaced

workloadFields.label: Traffic pattern
workloadFields.description: Shape of the offered load over time

workloadFields.label: Distinct keys
workloadFields.description: Number of distinct keys requests touch (used by TTL cache models)

workloadFields.label: Key skew (Zipf s)
workloadFields.description: Zipf exponent of key popularity (0 = uniform, ~1 = typical web skew)

workloadFields.label: Drain time
workloadFields.description: Time after arrivals stop to let in-flight requests finish (s). Empty = automatic.

workloadFields.label: Faults
workloadFields.description: Faults injected during the run (outages, slowdowns, network latency)

tierNote: Behaviour based on documentation and illustrative numbers; not yet validated against measurements.
